name: Orchid extract
lead: Orchid extract refers to preparations from various orchid species used in cosmetics, most often marketed as antioxidant or anti-aging botanicals in Asian skincare. The orchid family (Orchidaceae) is very large, so the term covers different species, such as Dendrobium and Phalaenopsis, with different chemistry.[1]

Published research on orchid extracts is mostly laboratory and animal work. Examples include a Phalaenopsis extract tested in a cell-culture model of sun-induced pigment spots and a Dendrobium extract tested in rats for bone loss.[2][3] Patent filings describe Dendrobium chrysotoxum extract for anti-aging cosmetic use.[4]
No human clinical trial of an orchid extract for skin appearance was found.

paras: Orchids are one of the largest plant families. Beyond ornamental use, some orchid parts have culinary and perfumery roles: the ground tubers of terrestrial orchids make the drink and ice cream known as salep, and vanilla comes from the seed pods of Vanilla orchids.[1] Cosmetic orchid extracts are a separate category and are typically derived from species such as Dendrobium or Phalaenopsis.

A 2016 study reported that a Phalaenopsis orchid extract inhibited WNT1-induced differentiation of immature melanocyte precursors in a co-culture model designed to mimic solar lentigo (sun spots).[2] A 2012 patent filing describes an anti-aging composition containing Dendrobium chrysotoxum extract.[4] A Dendrobium officinale extract prevented bone loss in ovariectomized rats and inhibited osteoclast differentiation in vitro, which concerns osteoporosis rather than skin.[3]
No studies found. Related work on orchid extracts is limited to cell-culture and animal studies, as described above, and patent filings.

card.summary: Antioxidant K-beauty botanical from several orchid species; support is limited to lab, animal and patent material.
card.note: Species vary widely and no human skin trial was found.

quick.overview:
Orchid extract is a botanical cosmetic ingredient, usually marketed as antioxidant and anti-aging. It is not a single substance: different orchid species are used.

Published work consists of cell and animal studies plus patents.
quick.mechanism: Proposed mechanisms are antioxidant activity and, in one cell model, reduced melanocyte precursor differentiation.
quick.risks: No safety data specific to cosmetic orchid extracts were found in the sources reviewed.
